First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =c\,⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩ \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =⟨\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3c{t}^{2},\,2c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{t}=\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}} \\ {t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2} \\ 2t+2=2c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2t.$ Substituting into the third equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+2 & =2\cdot (2t) \\ 2t+2 & =4t \\ 2t-2 & =0 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the second equation ${t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2}.$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$ These values also satisfy the second equation. 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\sqrt{1}\,,\,{1}^{3}+5\,,\,2(1)+2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,6,\,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,6,4).$
